episodes.168861: A nearly stationary boundary oriented from north to south set up over the area. Showers and thunderstorms developed along the boundary. Storm motion was also north to south, which allowed for storms to train over the same locations, resulting in instances of flooding and flash flooding.
episodes.168873: A nearly stationary boundary oriented from north to south set up over the area. Showers and thunderstorms developed along the boundary. Storm motion was also north to south, which allowed for storms to train over the same locations, resulting in isolated instances of flooding.
episodes.168874: A nearly stationary boundary oriented from north to south set up over the area. Showers and thunderstorms developed along the boundary. Storm motion was also north to south, which allowed for storms to train over the same locations, resulting in isolated instances of flooding.
episodes.168902: Diurnal heating, along with a weak upper shortwave moving south over the region on the eastern periphery of an upper ridge, and convergence along surface boundaries, led to a cluster of thunderstorms that shifted south over the central Midlands of SC, some of which reached severe limits.
episodes.168907: A surge of moisture from Tropical Storm Celia which was off the west coast of Mexico near 17N moved over a hot and unstable airmass which was situated over central California. This resulted in scattered showers and thunderstorms over the area on June 22 which was also the first significant precipitation event for the area in two months.  Due to the convective nature of the precipitation, rainfall amounts varied; but a few thunderstorms produced one to two tenths of an inch of rainfall in the San Joaquin Valley.  Some stations in the Tehachapi Mountains and the south end of the upper Sierra picked up between a  quarter and three quarters of an inch of rainfall.  Some of the thunderstorms produced strong outflow winds and dry microbursts which resulted in several trees and power lines being downed.
episodes.168918: Isolated afternoon thunderstorms developed along the sea breeze, and one thunderstorm that moved across the Cape in Brevard County produced a couple of strong wind gusts.
episodes.168923: A Low Pressure system tracking across southern Saskatchewan dragged a cold front through Northeast Montana.  The front would trigger some strong to severe thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours.
episodes.168937: A cyclic supercell developed across central Kansas, during the evening of June 23rd, 2022. A total of 6 tornadoes touched down during the evening. There were winds that overturned a semitrailer and camper on Interstate 70. Additionally up to ping ping ball sized hail fell.
episodes.169036: The surface synoptic set-up on June 22, 2022 was similar to that of the severe weather event just 6 days earlier, as a north-south stationary boundary bisected central Pennsylvania ahead of a cold front approaching from the Great Lakes. To the west of the north-south stationary boundary, the airmass over western Pennsylvania was very warm and humid with strong instability. Scattered thunderstorms first developed during the early afternoon over the south-central mountains, with additional activity developing farther north over the central mountains and over western Pennsylvania later in the afternoon.  By early evening, the primary focus for convection was found just ahead of the front as it pushed into western Pennsylvania. Damaging winds were the dominant severe weather type, with only one report of marginally severe hail. One thunderstorm brought locally heavy rain to Altoona and Hollidaysburg resulting in minor flooding.
episodes.169093: A strongly unstable airmass in a moderately sheared environment squeezed between two fronts resulted in several clusters of destructive thunderstorms. The most intense thunderstorms propagated north to south along a stalled front dividing very unstable air near and west of Interstate 95, from notably more stable air closer to the Chesapeake Bay.||The event was unusual not only because of the intensity of the thunderstorms, but because they moved in a north to south direction, even propagating south-southwestward at times.
episodes.169114: An upper-level low located over the Great Basin produced cooler than normal 500 mb temperature of between -9 and -10C and also some upper-level diffluence with a 50-60 kt jet at upper-levels. Moisture levels were also above normal with precipitable water values between 1.0-1.3 inches. The combination of all of these factors resulted in sufficient instability with MLCAPE values approaching 1000 J/KG while DCAPE values were approaching 1500 J/KG. Thunderstorms began to develop during the early to mid-afternoon hours across most of southern and central Arizona, with strong to locally damaging winds as well as dense blowing dust being the main hazards along with locally heavy rainfall. One of the damaged areas came just northwest of Stanfield, where there were multiple downed power poles as well as a rolled over RV. There were also visible photos from social media as well as from seasoned storm chasers of a couple of landspouts, one near damaged area just northwest of Stanfield and another over Buckeye. With respect to the landspout that developed just northwest of Stanfield, there was no confirmation that it was responsible for the damage observed, which most likely was due to downburst wind. No injuries were reported with these thunderstorms.
episodes.169222: During the late afternoon, and early evening of Thursday, June 23rd, a small complex of storms developed in central Minnesota. These storms were developing along an 850mb confluent boundary with an above normal plume of PWATs of 1.25. Due to a high freezing level, a sounding profile suggesting efficient warm-rain processes dominated.  With back-building storms across central Minnesota, rainfall amounts were excessive. Some areas received up to 7 inches of rainfall before rates diminished during the pre-dawn hours. The worst areas were across Todd, Morrison, Stearns and Benton Counties where a band of 3 to 6 inches fell before 4 am. In addition to the heavy rainfall, and flash flooding, the initial hazard was isolated large hail.
episodes.169356: Strong storms that produced damaging winds developed the evening of June 22, 2022. A broken line of showers and storms developed between Cleveland and Pittsburgh just before 3pm and continue to advances southeast along the axis of a trough entering from the north. Dry conditions under ridging hours ahead of the showers and storms helped prime the environment. Mean level CAPE before convective was between 3000-3500J/kg, and steep lapse rates near the surface (7.5 to 8.0C/km) help with strong damaging updrafts.
episodes.169571: With afternoon heating, upslope downpours affected leeward areas of the Big Island.  The rain produced small stream and drainage ditch flooding, and ponding on roadways.  No significant property damage or injuries were reported.
episodes.169641: A storm tracked southeast from Kentucky into southwest Virginia, producing downed trees and widespread power outages in Wise County.
episodes.169742: A surface low situated over the Great Lakes tracked eastward toward New England, with a trailing cold front that pushed eastward towards the Commonwealth. SPC had eastern Kentucky in a marginal category for severe weather throughout the day, with the main threat being wind. A watch was issued for the forecast area in the late afternoon before severe storms associated with the front moved through.
episodes.169784: Scattered afternoon thunderstorms occurred during the afternoon with one producing damaging winds.
episodes.170159: On the afternoon of June 22nd, a cold front made eastward progress into the Middle Ohio Valley, which served as the main contributor behind strong to severe thunderstorms in West Virginia. Optimal moisture levels and warm temperatures ahead of the front helped to promote these storms by the early afternoon on the 22nd, which spanned into the evening time frame as well. ||While an instance of quarter sized hail was observed in Nicholas County, the bulk of the strong to severe storms resulted in damaging wind gusts that knocked down trees in several areas across the state. Heavier downpours also caused high water to be observed along local roadwyas in Nicholas and Barbour Counties.
episodes.170190: A slow moving cold front pushed into the St. Lawrence Valley and northern Adirondacks during the morning hours of June 23, 2022. Bands of showers and thunderstorms, some with moderate to locally heavy rainfall were observed in this region, especially in the vicinity of Malone, NY.
episodes.170223: A surface trough settled across NE FL in the afternoon and evening trailed by drier air. A few strong to severe storms impacted Marion county near the frontal zone which produced strong downburst winds.
episodes.170506: A lone thunderstorm brought severe hail to Mount Sherman in Newton County on the 23rd.
episodes.170930: Clear skies through the day with southwesterly flow at the surface lead to rapid heating and moisture advection across the Northland. This lead to the development of thunderstorms during the afternoon hours that were prolific hail producers across the region with the largest hail bring the size of baseballs. Additionally, slow storm movement along with training storms near Pine Center produced some flash flooding.
episodes.171150: Unusually deep moisture for late June was located over southwest New Mexico with some slow moving storms dropping significant rains across the area which led to flash flooding around Mesquite and Hillsboro.
episodes.171412: A land spout was seen east of Winona near Twin Arrows for about 15 minutes.
episodes.171521: Thunderstorms moved northeast across southeast Arizona. One storm produced winds that downed power lines in Catalina.
episodes.171522: Thunderstorms moved north across southeast Arizona. Thunderstorm winds produced a wall of dust along I-10 in Pinal County.  Other storms produced heavy rain and flash flooding in the Baboquivari Mountains.
episodes.171677: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed across Middle Tennessee during the afternoon and evening hours on June 22. One report of wind damage was received in Overton County.
episodes.171699: CAPE values of over 1000 J/kg with DCAPE about the same allowed for severe wind gusts.  Shear was weak and lapse rates were modest at best so most storms were below severe limits.
episodes.171740: Thunderstorms developed across southeast Mississippi and produced strong winds.
episodes.171741: Strong thunderstorms developed across southwest Alabama and produced strong wind gusts.
episodes.171830: A weakening cold front approaching the area from the Ohio River Valley interacted with an unstable environment in southwest Virginia to spawn scattered severe thunderstorms. A few of the storms in the Virginia Piedmont produced damaging winds.
episodes.171831: A weakening cold front approaching the area from the Ohio River Valley interacted with an unstable environment in southeast West Virginia to spawn scattered severe thunderstorms which produced damaging winds.
episodes.171847: Monsoonal moisture resulted in thunderstorms with gusty outflow winds in portions northern Utah, as well as flash flooding in portions of southern Utah.

The Panoche Road RAWS measured a peak wind gust of 63 mph from a thunderstorm.

The water level rose above flood stage along the Accotink Creek a Strathmeade Springs. The water level crested at 252.44 feet at 2:00 AM EST on the 23rd of June. Woodburn Road was covered by more than six inches of water and portions of the Cross Country Trail were flooded.
Beach Drive was closed between Connecticut Avenue and Kensington Parkway.
The water level along Rock Creek at Sherrill Drive rose above flood stage, cresting at 7.16 feet at 1:45 AM EST. Water reached several portions of the Valley Trail between picnic areas 7 and 10.

Showers and thunderstorms trained across portions of northeastern Franklin County, NY in the vicinity of Malone and the hamlet of Whippleville. One home in Whippleville was evacuated due to high water from a creek feeding into the nearby Salmon River. A driveway crossing the creek at the residence was overwhelmed and clogged by debris, impounding water, which quickly rose, flooding the residence. County Road 25, 2 miles south-southeast of Whippleville was also closed due to high water as a farm pond and connected drainage overflowed onto the highway. Additionally, a portion of Webster Road, approximately  1 mile southwest of Whippleville near the Malone Fish and Game Club was closed due to high water.

Capitol Reef National Park reported SR-24 was impassable near milepost 83 due to flood waters from grand wash. Scenic drive was also closed, and the parking lot at the Grand Wash trailhead flooded. The flooding stranded nearly 60 people, and trapped or washed away several vehicles. Numerous water rescues were conducted by Utah Department of Public Safety helicopter operations to bring people to safety.
High winds downed multiple trees.
Multiple trees and powerlines were down along NE Jacksonville rd extending from 49th st to  90th st. Time was estimated by radar.
Nearly 2 inches of rain in less than 2 hours over the Contreras burn scar caused a 1-2 ft debris flow across State Highway 386 to Kitt Peak.

Multiple trees downed or snapped, power lines downed and power outages near Midway rd, bahia rd and spring rd. Large trees of about 8 to 10 ft in circumference were snapped at the trunk. Time was estimated by radar. Damage due to downburst winds.
Multiple trees and powerlines down along SE 55th place. Trees and powerlines were reported to be twisted together. Damage was from downburst winds. Time was estimated by radar.
An estimated 50 to 60 mph winds occurred.
Downed power pole. Winds were estimated at around 70 mph. No injuries were reported.
A funnel cloud was observed from SE 175th lane in Summerfield, FL looking to the north. The funnel cloud was reported to be over Lake Weir.
A land spout was reported near Interstate 40 east of Winona near The Twin Arrows Trading Post.  It persisted for 10-15 minutes. Pictures were posted on social media.

Multiple storm chaser photos show a landspout tornado developed northwest of Stanfield. It appeared to be moving northeast along a thunderstorm outflow through open farm fields. The exact location, timing, path length, and width were all estimated based on the photos and radar. It is unknown if the landspout caused any property or crop damage and no damage survey was conducted. An RV did flip and around 50 power poles did fall in this area, but these reports were attributed to downburst winds due to nearly all power poles falling to the north. No injuries were reported.
High winds downed a tree on a mobile home.
High winds downed trees and large limbs in northern Clarke county.

Multiple reports from storm chasers and local media of multiple downed power poles, trees, flipped irrigation pivots, and a rolled RV along and just east of SR-347, northwest of Stanfield. The local utility company reported around 50 downed power poles across the area, most of which were blown toward the north. There was a confirmed landspout in the general area as well, however, there was no evidence that it was the cause of any of the damage. Therefore, the downburst winds are being treated as the official cause of the damages. Winds were estimated at around 70 mph after discussion with the utility company. No injuries were reported.
A thunderstorm and associated outflow produced a measured wind gust of 58 mph by the UPR Lucin2 Railroad Sensor.
A couple of trees and large branches were reported down in Roaring River State Park.
The St. Marie mesonet site (07MT) recorded a 60 mph thunderstorm wind gust.
Bull Creek flowed across the road near Main Street, bringing with it large debris.
Brief touchdown in open country.

Heavy rain of 1.5 to 3 inches in less than 3 hours caused flash flooding along Empire Ranch Rd.
A thunderstorm and associated outflow resulted in a peak wind gust of 59 mph being measured at the Dugway Target R weather observation station.

Thunderstorms and associated outflows resulted in multiple strong wind gusts at the Dugway Simpson Springs weather observing station over a short period of time. The initial wind gust of 66 mph was the peak wind gust, with lesser gusts of 59 mph and 61 mph noted before winds subsided.
A semitrailer and camper were blown over on Interstate 70 near mile marker 195 according to the Kansas Highway Patrol.
Brief touchdown in open country.

An initial gust of 60 mph was recorded, with strong winds persisting for 15 minutes before a peak wind gust of 65 mph was measured. Winds began subsiding thereafter.

Severe thunderstorm downburst winds produced a swath of damage which included numerous trees down in several locations, generally stretching from near Lebanon south to areas SW of Winnsboro, generally along and just east of Jackson Creek Rd.  Trees were downed on Armstrong Rd, Old Airport Rd and Jackson Creek Rd, Hwy 213 at Jackson Creek Rd, Corona Dr, Reservoir Rd and New Hope Rd, and at Chapell Town Rd at Reservoir Rd (SC S-20-70) where over a dozen trees were downed.   Times estimated.
